children: Asian markets rose Thursday, as investors shrugged off new U.S. tariff proposals and Wall Street recouped most of the sharp losses ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

The U.S. said Wednesday it would propose new tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production.

The proposed tariffs won't be added to earlier tariffs levied on 60 economies over forced labor concerns, as the higher of the two will apply. Also, the new rates would be put into place in January at the earliest, after a comment period for affected industries.
"The latest tariff move is therefore better viewed as a reconstruction and legal hardening of the Trump tariff regime than a fresh 'Liberation Day' shock," said MUFG analyst Lloyd Chan.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said the tariff announcement is "not as alarming as it looks," as the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than expected.
The measures, which look like a replacement for existing tariffs rather an escalation, soothed some investor concerns.

Sentiment also stabilized after a dramatic midday reversal in the U.S. overnight. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped as much as 4.6%, coming within 2 percentage points of bear-market territory, before recouping most of its losses to end 0.6% lower. The S&P 500 fell 0.3%, its ninth loss in 10 sessions, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3%.

Asia's tech-heavy markets, which suffered a selloff in the previous session, staged a major comeback on Thursday. Taiwan's Taiex rallied 2.0%, South Korea's Kospi rose 2.3% and Japan's Nikkei Stock Average was 1.5% higher.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 2.2% and China's Shanghai Composite Index was 0.4% higher.

Oil regained some momentum with continuing tensions in the Middle East. Renewed hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Houthi militants in Yemen have raised concerns over the security of Red Sea shipping routes, which have become increasingly important for Saudi oil exports amid disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz.
Supply concerns have resurfaced again due to attacks on Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure and renewed disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, OCBC's Sim Moh Siong said in a note.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude-oil futures rose 0.7% to $84.29 a barrel, while front-month Brent was up 0.4% at $95.00 a barrel.
